group/value: A good baseline is the reward you expect for this very question. One way to get it is to train a second model to predict it: a value model, a whole second network to train.
group/group: GRPO does without it. For each question, sample a group of G answers, here eight, and check each one: a reward, r, of one if it is right, zero if it is wrong.
group/mean: The group's mean reward is the baseline. Three of the eight are right, so it is zero point three seven five.
group/sub: Subtract it, as with any baseline. A right answer is one minus zero point three seven five: zero point six two five above it. A wrong one is zero point three seven five below.
group/std: Then divide by the group's standard deviation, how spread out its rewards are: here about zero point four eight four. That puts every question's advantages on a similar scale.
group/adv: Right answers get zero point six two five over zero point four eight four: one point two nine. Wrong ones get minus zero point three seven five over zero point four eight four: minus zero point seven seven. Each advantage is r minus the mean, over the standard deviation.
agree/hard: A right answer to a hard question, where only one of eight succeeds, earns a big push: two point six five. On an easy one, where seven of eight do, each right answer gets only zero point three eight.
agree/easy: If every answer in the group is right, each reward equals the mean, and every advantage is zero.
agree/none: Such a group teaches nothing, and the same goes when every answer is wrong. The standard deviation is zero then, so code adds a tiny number to it, and zero divided by that stays zero.
agree/sum: Within any group, the advantages add up to zero: probability moves from the worse answers to the better ones.
agree/cost: There is no value model to train. The price is sampling several answers for every question.
try/p1: Try one. GRPO samples five answers, with rewards zero, one, zero, zero and zero, and a standard deviation of zero point four. What is the advantage of answer one, counting from zero?
try/mean: One of the five is right, so the mean is one fifth: zero point two.
try/sub: Answer one got a reward of one: one minus zero point two is zero point eight.
try/div: Divide by the standard deviation: zero point eight over zero point four is two.
try/all: Each wrong answer gets zero minus zero point two, over zero point four: minus zero point five. So the whole group's advantages are minus zero point five, two, then minus zero point five three more times.
